Text: The branch of physics called {{c1::mechanics}} is the study of {{c2::the motion of objects}}, together with force and energy.
Back Extra:
Why: the modern understanding of motion was established in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, above all by Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton.

Ex: a baseball's flight, a braking automobile, a jogger, and even the motion of the Sun and Moon are all mechanics.

Text: Mechanics divides into two parts, {{c1::kinematics}}, the description of how objects move, and {{c2::dynamics}}, which deals with force and why objects move as they do.
Back Extra:
Cue: kinematics asks how; dynamics asks why — force is the word that separates them.

Ex: working out how far a braking car travels is kinematics; explaining that a force is what slowed it is dynamics.

Text: Translational motion is {{c1::movement of an object without any rotation}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "For now we only discuss objects that move without rotating. Such motion is called translational motion."

Parts: trans- (across) + -lation (carrying) — the whole object is carried from one place to another.

Distinguish: rotation is spinning about an axis; a falling pinecone that also spins is doing both at once.

Text: In physics, a particle is {{c1::an idealized point with no size}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "We will often use the concept, or model, of an idealized particle which is considered to be a mathematical point with no spatial extent."

Why: a point has no size, so it cannot spin — a point particle can undergo only translational motion.

Cue: a real object counts as a particle whenever only its overall motion matters — a billiard ball, or even a spacecraft traveling toward the Moon.
verified_by: lexicon anchor kept external: --find matched p61 "particle is moving toward decreasing acceleration ... is the slope of" — graph-reading prose, not a definition

Text: Any measurement of position, distance, or speed must be made with respect to a {{c1::reference frame}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: a person walking toward the front of a train moves at 5 km/h with respect to the train, but at 85 km/h with respect to the ground when the train travels 80 km/h.

Pitfall: a speed quoted with nothing to measure it against is incomplete — "80 km/h" only means something once you say relative to what.

Text: An object's {{c1::displacement}} is {{c2::its change in position}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: distance is the whole path length actually traveled; displacement is only how far the object ends up from where it started.

Ex: walking 70 m east and then 30 m west covers 100 m of distance but gives a displacement of only 40 m east.

Pitfall: the displacement may not equal the total distance traveled.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The change in any quantity means {{c1::the final value minus the initial value}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the Greek letter Δ (delta) in front of a symbol is shorthand for "change in", so \(\Delta x = x_2 - x_1\) is the displacement and \(\Delta t = t_2 - t_1\) is the elapsed time.

Pitfall: the order matters — always final minus initial, never the reverse, or every sign flips.

Text: In physics, a quantity's magnitude is {{c1::its size or numerical value, apart from direction}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "the blue arrow represents the displacement whose magnitude is 40 m and whose direction is to the right (east)."

Distinguish: magnitude answers how much; direction answers which way — a vector needs both.

Pitfall: a magnitude is never negative; in one-dimensional motion the minus sign sits in front of the magnitude and carries the direction.

Text: A vector is {{c1::a quantity having both size and direction}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Displacement is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Such quantities are called vectors."

Cue: vectors are drawn as arrows — the arrow's length is the magnitude, the way it points is the direction.

Distinguish: distance is just a number with units; displacement is a vector, so it also names a direction.

Text: An object's {{c1::average speed}} is its {{c2::total distance traveled divided by the time elapsed}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: average speed counts every metre covered, including any doubling back, and is always a plain positive number with units.

Ex: a car that travels 240 km in 3 h has an average speed of 80 km/h.

Pitfall: averaging two speeds does not give the average speed — 50 km/h for one leg and 100 km/h for another does not come to 75 km/h.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Speed is simply a positive number with units, while velocity signifies both how fast an object is moving and {{c1::the direction in which it is moving}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: in ordinary language "speed" and "velocity" are used interchangeably; in physics they are not.

Pitfall: because velocity carries direction, its sign matters — an object moving left along the x axis has a negative velocity, while its speed stays positive.

Text: Unlike speed, velocity is not just a number — in physics velocity is classified as a {{c1::vector}}.
Back Extra:
Why: velocity carries a direction as well as a magnitude, and a quantity with both is a vector.

Cue: vectors are drawn as arrows, so a velocity can be pictured as an arrow whose length is the speed.

Distinguish: speed has no direction attached, so speed is not a vector.

Text: Average velocity is defined in terms of {{c1::displacement}}, rather than total distance traveled.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: average speed uses the total distance along the path; average velocity uses displacement, so the two differ whenever the motion reverses.

Ex: walking 70 m east then 30 m west in 70 s gives an average speed of 1.4 m/s but an average velocity of only 0.57 m/s.

Pitfall: average speed is not necessarily equal to the magnitude of the average velocity.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Give the equation for average velocity in words: {{c1::displacement / time elapsed}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: written out in full, the same equation is (final position − initial position) / time elapsed.

Distinguish: average speed uses the length of the path actually walked; average velocity uses only how far the endpoint sits from the start.

Pitfall: displacement can be negative, so average velocity can be negative — average speed never is.

Text: The elapsed time, or time interval, is written {{c1::\(\Delta t = t_2 - t_1\)}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(t_1\) is the earlier (initial) time and \(t_2\) the later (final) time, so \(\Delta t\) is always final minus initial.

Cue: \(\Delta\) is read "change in", and the same pattern gives the displacement \(\Delta x = x_2 - x_1\).

Pitfall: it is always worth choosing and stating the interval — the elapsed time is the time that passes during the chosen period of observation.

Text: Give the equation for average velocity in symbols: {{c1::\(\bar v = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(\bar v\) is the average velocity, and the bar over the v is the standard symbol for "average"; \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are the positions at the earlier time \(t_1\) and the later time \(t_2\); \(\Delta x\) is the displacement and \(\Delta t\) the elapsed time.

Pitfall: if \(x_2\) is less than \(x_1\) the object moved left, \(\Delta x\) is negative, and so is the average velocity — the sign carries the direction.

Text: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a single instant, defined precisely as {{c1::the average velocity}} taken over {{c2::an infinitesimally short time interval}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity is the number, with units, that a speedometer shows.

Meaning: "infinitesimally short" means the elapsed time \(\Delta t\) is allowed to shrink toward zero.

Distinguish: average velocity is taken over a whole finite interval, so a car with a 75 km/h average was almost certainly not moving at exactly 75 km/h at every instant.

Text: Give the equation defining instantaneous velocity: {{c1::\(v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(\Delta x\) is the displacement during the short interval \(\Delta t\), and \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\) means the ratio \(\Delta x / \Delta t\) is evaluated as \(\Delta t\) shrinks toward zero.

Distinguish: the symbol for instantaneous velocity is a plain \(v\); average velocity gets a bar, \(\bar v\).

Pitfall: from here on, "velocity" on its own means instantaneous velocity.

Text: An object is accelerating whenever {{c1::its velocity is changing}}. Acceleration specifies how rapidly that change happens.
Back Extra:
Ex: a car whose velocity increases in magnitude from zero to 80 km/h is accelerating.

Pitfall: acceleration tells how quickly the velocity changes, whereas velocity tells how quickly the position changes — do not swap them.

Distinguish: a zero velocity does not mean a zero acceleration — a car at rest with your foot going down on the gas has \(v = 0\) but \(a \ne 0\).

Text: Give the equation for average acceleration in words: {{c1::change of velocity / time elapsed}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the "change of velocity" is the final velocity minus the initial velocity.

Distinguish: average velocity is built from a change in position; average acceleration is built from a change in velocity.

Pitfall: the units come out as velocity units per unit time — m/s per second, which is written m/s².

Text: Give the equation for average acceleration in symbols: {{c1::\(\bar a = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(\bar a\) is the average acceleration, the bar meaning "average"; \(v_1\) is the velocity at the earlier time \(t_1\) and \(v_2\) the velocity at the later time \(t_2\); \(\Delta v\) is the change in velocity and \(\Delta t\) the elapsed time.

Ex: a car going from rest to 75 km/h in 5.0 s has \(\bar a\) = 15 km/h per second, which is 4.2 m/s².

Pitfall: acceleration is a vector, so in one-dimensional motion a plus or minus sign carries its direction — usually right is +, left is −.

Text: Instantaneous acceleration at a given instant is defined as {{c1::the average acceleration}} taken over {{c2::an infinitesimally short time interval}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: it is built exactly the way instantaneous velocity is — take the average over an interval, then let that interval shrink toward zero.

Meaning: the \(\Delta v\) involved is the very small change in velocity during the very short time interval \(\Delta t\).

Distinguish: instantaneous acceleration is a plain \(a\); average acceleration carries a bar, \(\bar a\).

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Give the equation for instantaneous acceleration: {{c1::\(a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(\Delta v\) is the very small change in velocity during the very short time interval \(\Delta t\), and \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\) means the ratio is evaluated as \(\Delta t\) shrinks toward zero.

Distinguish: the same limit applied to \(\Delta x / \Delta t\) instead gives the instantaneous velocity.

Cue: drop the limit and the bar comes back — over a finite interval it is \(\bar a\).

Text: An object is decelerating whenever {{c1::the magnitude of its velocity is decreasing}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: deceleration does not mean that the acceleration is negative. A car moving to the left along a decreasing x axis and slowing down has a positive acceleration.

Ex: a car moving right along the +x axis and braking has a negative acceleration; the same car moving left and braking has a positive one.

Cue: what makes it deceleration is that the speed is dropping, not the sign of \(a\).

Text: When an object is decelerating, its velocity and its acceleration point in {{c1::opposite::the same/opposite}} directions.
Back Extra:
Why: an acceleration pointing against the motion is exactly what makes the speed drop.

Ex: a car moving right at 15.0 m/s that brakes to 5.0 m/s in 5.0 s has \(\bar a = -2.0\) m/s² — velocity to the right, acceleration to the left.

Distinguish: when velocity and acceleration point the same way, the object speeds up instead.

Text: For motion with constant acceleration, give the kinematic equation for the velocity \(v\) after an elapsed time \(t\): {{c1::\(v = v_0 + at\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(v\) is the velocity at time \(t\); \(v_0\) (read "v-naught") is the initial velocity, its value at \(t = 0\); \(a\) is the constant acceleration; \(t\) is the elapsed time.

Cue: this is the only one of the four with no position term in it at all.

Pitfall: the four kinematic equations hold only while the acceleration \(a\) stays constant.

Text: For motion with constant acceleration, give the kinematic equation for the position \(x\) after an elapsed time \(t\): {{c1::\(x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(x\) is the position at time \(t\); \(x_0\) (read "x-naught") is the initial position, its value at \(t = 0\); \(v_0\) is the initial velocity; \(a\) is the constant acceleration; \(t\) is the elapsed time.

Cue: \(x\) is a position rather than a distance, and \(x - x_0\) is the displacement.

Pitfall: setting \(x_0 = 0\) shortens it to \(x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2\), but only once you have actually put the origin at the starting point. The equation holds only while \(a\) stays constant.

Text: For motion with constant acceleration, give the kinematic equation that relates velocity to position with no time term in it: {{c1::\(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(v\) is the velocity at position \(x\); \(v_0\) is the initial velocity at the initial position \(x_0\); \(a\) is the constant acceleration; \(x - x_0\) is the displacement.

Cue: reach for this one whenever the elapsed time \(t\) is neither known nor asked for.

Pitfall: the four kinematic equations hold only while the acceleration \(a\) stays constant.

Text: For motion with constant acceleration, give the kinematic equation for the average velocity \(\bar v\) in terms of the initial and final velocities: {{c1::\(\bar v = \frac{v + v_0}{2}\)}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: \(\bar v\) is the average velocity over the interval; \(v_0\) is the initial velocity and \(v\) the final velocity.

Distinguish: this midpoint shortcut holds only for constant acceleration, whereas the general definition of average velocity works for any motion at all.

Pitfall: the four kinematic equations hold only while the acceleration \(a\) stays constant.

Text: At a given location on the Earth and in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with {{c1::the same constant acceleration}}.
Back Extra:
Why: this is Galileo's specific contribution to our understanding of the motion of falling objects.

Cue: both conditions matter — a given location on the Earth, and no air resistance.

Pitfall: air resistance is usually small enough to neglect, but it becomes noticeable even on a reasonably heavy object once the velocity becomes large.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Earth is given the symbol \(g\), and its magnitude is approximately {{c1::9.80 m/s²}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: in British units \(g\) is about 32 ft/s².

Cue: \(g\) varies slightly with latitude and elevation on the Earth's surface, but the variations are small enough to ignore for most purposes.

Pitfall: \(g\) is an acceleration, not a force, and the 9.80 value is for the Earth's surface — it does not hold out in space.

Text: Acceleration due to gravity is a vector like any acceleration, and its direction is {{c1::downward, toward the center of the Earth}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: because \(g\) has a direction, its sign depends on which way you chose to call positive — \(y\) may be taken as positive upward or downward, but you must be consistent throughout a problem.

Cue: for freely falling objects, use \(g\) in place of \(a\) and \(y\) in place of \(x\), taking \(y_0 = 0\) unless stated otherwise.
